articles.text: The Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) and the City of Piedmont co-hosted the 25th Annual MLK Day Celebration on January 17 honoring the life and legacy of Civil Rights Leader Martin Luther King, Jr. Due to COVID and Omicron, this year’s event was virtual and available via Zoom. The program included five guest speakers: U.S Representative Barbara Lee; Dr. Clayborne Carson, Founding Director of the Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute; Anna Malaika Tubbs, author of The Three Mothers; Assembly member Buffy Wicks; and Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King. The theme of this year’s program was “Changing Souls, Changing Lives, and Creating Community.” Drawing upon a quote from Dr. King, which calls for us to “create a beloved community,” each featured speaker touched on what a beloved community means. The celebration was founded and organized by Piedmont resident Lois Corrin. This year, she was joined by her daughter Camillie Lafayette in moderating the program and introducing program speakers. articles.text: Open letter to Piedmont community. Editor: Recently, I was surprised to learn of Piedmont High School’s decision to release the head football coach, Jerome Johnson. I am concerned about the future of the program. Our sons played for three different coaches from 2016-2021 and coach Johnson was outstanding. I was the JV and Varsity Team Parent and worked closely with each coach. I am grateful that Coach Johnson provided stability and leadership during the last three seasons. He was knowledgeable, student-centered, patient, and inspirational. We appreciate Coach Johnson’s dedication to our community and are dismayed with the way he has been treated. Football was truly the highlight of our family’s high school experience and the most valuable growth experience for our sons. They learned discipline, teamwork, leadership, how to overcome disappointment, and humility. Today, a new group of players has the opportunity to play under the lights at Witter Field. Parents have the opportunity to share in the Highlander pride of a 100+ year tradition. We hope that the Piedmont community recognizes the value of the football program to the development of young players – from flag football in middle school to the JV and Varsity teams. Each team is a developmental milestone and players should aspire to play at the highest level for their ability. The thought of discontinuing the Varsity team is not only disappointing to the current upperclassmen but also implies that younger players aren’t good enough to carry on the tradition of sophomores on varsity. Our experience shows that with the right coaching, discipline and physical conditioning, encouraging parents, and a supportive administration the varsity team will continue to teach valuable lessons to our players. I sincerely hope this discussion about the future of the football program moves to the hiring of a head coach, recruiting players, and scheduling an off-season workout schedule. Let’s move forward with confidence and conviction. –Mary Alice McNeil Ed. note: Mary Alice McNeil is a PHS alum and parent of two former football players, Billy McNeil (Class of 2020), and Tommy McNeil (Class of 2021).
articles.title: Let’s get the football program back on track

articles.text: The American Red Cross announced on January 11 that it is facing a national blood crisis, describing it as “the worst blood shortage in more than a decade.” Dangerously low blood supply levels are creating a risk to patient care across the country, the agency explained in a press release, and is forcing doctors “to make difficult decisions about who receives blood transfusions and who will need to wait until more products become available.” Blood donations are critically needed at this time, especially type O blood donors; however, donors of all types are encouraged to make an appointment now to give in the weeks ahead. “Winter weather across the country and the recent surge of COVID-19 cases are compounding the already-dire situation facing the blood supply,” said Dr. Baia Lasky, medical director for the Red Cross. “Please, if you are eligible, make an appointment to give blood or platelets in the days and weeks ahead to ensure no patient is forced to wait for critical care.” Over the next few weeks, about 54% of donation appointments remain unfilled in the Red Cross’s Northern California Coastal Region. Due to COVID-19 and challenges presented by the pandemic, the agency has seen about a 10% overall decline in donations as well as ongoing blood drive cancellations due to staff shortages. To donate blood at the Blood Bank at 6230 Claremont Avenue in Oakland, call (800) 733-2767. articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont launched its Defending Democracy Speaker Series on January 11 with a presentation on Voting Rights by Carol Moon Goldberg, president of the League of Women Voters of California. Upcoming events in this series include Ranked Choice Voting with Rob Richie on February 10, Election Law and the Supreme Court with Erwin Chemerinsky on March 1, International Perspective on U.S. Democracy with Dr. Fiona Hill on March 30, and Election Subversion and Disinformation with Rick Hasen on April 5. The series is co-sponsored by Leagues across the country in Collier County, Florida; Gunnison Valley, Colorado; Oakland, California; The Pikes Peak Region, Colorado; Portland, Oregon; Pueblo, Colorado; Santa Barbara, California; and Solano County, California. Goldberg opened her presentation with a brief history of voting rights in California and in the U.S. that highlighted the country’s expansion of the right to vote beyond white, male property owners. This expansion was marked by the ratification of the 13th, 14th, 15th and 19th Amendments to the Constitution, the 1965 Voting Rights Act, and the Help America Vote Act that provided funding to help The League’s work in California has been instrumental in laws being passed that protect voting rights, including some of those mentioned above and Prop. 7, which restores voting rights to people who are on parole. Many of them are taxpaying, contributing members of society who deserve a voice in their government. Goldberg closed her presentation with a focus on the current federal voting rights legislation and suggestions for how the public can support voting rights. The Freedom to Vote Act protects and expands the right to vote, decreases the influence of money in politics and curbs partisan gerrymandering. The John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act (JLVRAA) effectively restores section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 that was gutted by the Supreme Court in Shelby County v. Holder in 2013. The JLVRAA would require federal preclearance for certain changes to state voting laws and would result in federal voting rights protections to counter racial discrimination. The League is part of a coalition of 230 organizations supporting these federal bills. articles.text: Starting on January 24, Piedmont High School will try starting classes at 8:30 a.m. instead of 8 a.m. The pilot schedule will last for four weeks, until February 18. It will also include later dismissal times and the addition of a Homeroom period at PHS. The change comes in preparation for new California Senate Bill 328, which will require public high schools in California to start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. as of fall 2022. The bill also requires middle schools to not start until 8:00 a.m. Piedmont Middle School currently starts classes at 8:20 a.m. PMS is participating in a similar pilot schedule affecting dismissal times and adding a homeroom period. The new bell schedule was explained during a January 14 PHS Parent Club meeting. In the pilot schedule, school will begin at 8:30 a.m. Monday through Friday. On Mondays the last class period will end at 3:25 p.m.; Tuesdays and Thursday will go until 3:35 p.m. On Wednesdays and Fridays class will let out at 2:50 p.m. Piedmont High will remain on a block schedule with 90-minute classes Tuesday through Friday. On Mondays, students will continue to meet with all seven periods in 45-minute blocks. Lunch will continue to be 40 minutes but will start at 11:30 instead of 1:00 p.m.. Studies have shown that at the onset of puberty, the adolescent body does not produce melatonin or begin to feel sleepy until about 10:45 p.m., making an 8:00 a.m. start to school difficult while getting the 8-10 hours of required sleep for teens. On Wednesdays and Fridays the last period of the day will be a 45-minute Homeroom, required for all students. We d ne sd ay Home ro om will have “program” activities, including the mental health BESS survey, student presentations on consent, academic work, and a survey of the bell schedule. On Fridays students will have time to get extra help, make up tests, and complete science labs during Homeroom. Teachers may select students to attend their tutorial and students may request to attend a teacher’s specific tutorial. Homeroom is not a requirePiedmont High will temporarily begin school at 8:30 a.m., well in advance of the state’s requirement set for next fall. ment of the state legislation. “We are trying some things in the pilot [schedule], and we know that we are going to be able to do things a little differently if we commit to [homeroom] year long. Part of this is to keep things manageable [for teacher schedules],” said Littlefield. One logistical complication results from students, especially upper classmen, that have a free Period 7, but have to return to school at 2:05 p.m. on Wednesdays and Fridays instead of being dismissed at the start of lunch period. For these students, the high school is making the library available during 7th period and will also offer PCR COVID testing at that time. A later release time will also affect after-school extracurricular activities. Student athletes will be allowed to leave early to go to games. “There are a lot of different types of scenarios that can happen, and we will discuss them through this process,” said Littlefield. “We are going to try this and then we are going to learn from it and figure out what were the best practices of this and what do we really need to consider and reconsider.” California is the first state in the nation to move back the start time for high school students.

articles.text: On January 18 Piedmont School District announced that masks would again have to be worn outdoors on all school campuses. The mandate goes into effect today, Wednesday, January 19 and applies to all students, staff and anyone on campus. “Until indications are that the surge has peaked and the number of COVID cases within the District are in decline, the outdoor masking requirement for secondary students and staff will be temporarily reinstated effective Wednesday, January 19th,” declared superintendent Randy Booker in an email to parents of students in the district. The requirement also applies to family members while on campus during picking up or dropping of their students, or while visiting during the day. The decision will be revisited at the District’s Health & Safety Steering Committee meeting on January 26th. “I am aware this may not be a popular decision with everyone,” Booker acknowledged. “Our goal remains to protect in-person instruction and keep our students and staff on campus. It was the consensus of the Committee that under current conditions, this step back was the best way to continue accomplishing that goal,” he added. On November 1, 2021 the on-campus outdoor mask mandate was lifted by the school district for vaccinated 12-18 years olds. An outdoor mask mandate for elementary students during P.E., recess and anytime on campus remained in place at the time and has never been lifted since the return to school in 2020. No outdoor mask requirement at schools has been required by the California Department of Public Health. The initial decision to require masks outdoors, then their removal for the vaccinated, and now reinstated were recommendations by Booker With advice and consent by the District’s Health and Safety Steering Committee. Wearing masks outdoors has not been an action item by the school board. In the first semester, from August 20 through December 17, 2021, there were 25 student COVID cases reported and 13 among staff. From December 18 to January 10 there were 228 COVID cases reported by staff and students. From January 11-14 there were 33 new COVID cases reported by staff and students. As of Tuesday, January 18, 97% of all students in the school district were fully vaccinated.
articles.title: Outdoor mask mandate reinstated by school district

articles.text: In October 2021 Piedmont City Council approved the allocation of $100,000 in American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds to be used by the school district to hire a temporary, full-time nurse to assist with response to COVID. Since then, the district received no applications for the position, so School Superintendent Randy Booker has now requested to use the funds to hire health clerks. Funds from the American Rescue Plan Act are restricted and generally must be used to support public health response to the COVID-19 emergency. In October the City carved out ARPA funds that were intended to support the school district with a full-time nurse. City Administrator Sara Lillevand noted at the time that it was the school’s most important need. “At that time, the urgent need and request was for a full-time nurse to support [reopening] efforts. Unfortunately, they have not had luck fulfilling that position,” Lillevand told City Council members at a meeting yesterday, January 18. “With this big post-holiday surge [of Omicron], the district is doing a tremendous amount of testing to keep schools open. The [recent] request was to shift that funding for a similar need but different position – for multiple parttime health clerks. This request is very much in line with the intent of [the original] allocation.” School district health clerks provide support to school site operations with specific responsibilities under the direction of nurses or school principals, making the positions eligible for ARPA fund use. The revision was approved unanimously by four council members. “We want to do all we can to support the schools by keeping them open,” Mayor Teddy Gray King said.
articles.title: City Council approves using ARPA funds for PUSD to hire health clerks instead

The mandate goes into effect today, Wednesday, January 19 and applies to all students, staff and anyone on campus. “Until indications are that the surge has peaked and the number of COVID cases within the District are in decline, the outdoor masking requirement for secondary students and staff will be temporarily reinstated effective Wednesday, January 19th,” declared superintendent Randy Booker in an email to parents of students in the district. The requirement also applies to family members while on campus during picking up or dropping of their students, or while visiting during the day. The decision will be revisited at the District’s Health & Safety Steering Committee meeting on January 26th. “I am aware this may not be a popular decision with everyone,” Booker acknowledged. “Our goal remains to protect in-person instruction and keep our students and staff on campus. It was the consensus of the Committee that under current conditions, this step back was the best way to continue accomplishing that goal,” he added. On November 1, 2021 the on-campus outdoor mask mandate was lifted by the school district for vaccinated 12-18 years olds. An outdoor mask mandate for elementary students during P.E., recess and anytime on campus remained in place at the time and has never been lifted since the return to school in 2020. No outdoor mask requirement at schools has been required by the California Department of Public Health. The initial decision to require masks outdoors, then their removal for the vaccinated, and now reinstated were recommendations by Booker With advice and consent by the District’s Health and Safety Steering Committee. Wearing masks outdoors has not been an action item by the school board. In the first semester, from August 20 through December 17, 2021, there were 25 student COVID cases reported and 13 among staff. From December 18 to January 10 there were 228 COVID cases reported by staff and students. From January 11-14 there were 33 new COVID cases reported by staff and students. As of Tuesday, January 18, 97% of all students in the school district were fully vaccinated. Since then, the district received no applications for the position, so School Superintendent Randy Booker has now requested to use the funds to hire health clerks. Funds from the American Rescue Plan Act are restricted and generally must be used to support public health response to the COVID-19 emergency. In October the City carved out ARPA funds that were intended to support the school district with a full-time nurse. City Administrator Sara Lillevand noted at the time that it was the school’s most important need. “At that time, the urgent need and request was for a full-time nurse to support [reopening] efforts. Unfortunately, they have not had luck fulfilling that position,” Lillevand told City Council members at a meeting yesterday, January 18. “With this big post-holiday surge [of Omicron], the district is doing a tremendous amount of testing to keep schools open. articles.text: “There’s a problem with how we teach math in the United States,” explained Carlos Trujillo, Chair of Bishop O’Dowd’s Math Department. “The standard course sequence dates back to the Industrial Revolution. It’s not setting students up to master the skills they need to succeed in today’s world.” Last year, in accordance with leading-edge research from the Stanford Graduate School of Education, The University of Chicago, and a growing cadre of mathematicians, data scientists, teachers, and education policy leaders, O’Dowd’s Math Department developed a two-year geometry, algebra, and trigonometry sequence – an innovative course remodel designed to prepare students to be problem solvers in today’s tech and data economy. As it stands now, most U.S. math students learn a sequence of Algebra 1 (one year), Geometry (one year), Algebra 2 (one year). “This math track is like learning to play piano one year, switching to cello for another year, then going back to piano as though you never stopped practicing,” Trujillo said. The sequence doesn’t support a true command of fundamental math concepts. “It’s how students get frustrated with math,” Trujillo noted. Second, this sequence usually doesn’t create enough time for students to take multiple upper division courses, like Data Science and Multivariable Calculus. “These are the courses that have Carlos Trujillo, O’Dowd High School Math Chair, teaches Advanced Placement Calculus. a big payoff for students,” Trujillo said. “They start solving real world problems, thinking creatively, and strengthening their college applications.” O’Dowd’s two-year math sequence is focused on students mastering the concepts they need to be successful. “We don’t want students who just know how to do the mechanics.” Trujillo stated. “We want them to gain the technical vocabulary, notational fluency, the analytical skills, and the conceptual thinking that matter for problem solving. It’s like an exponential function. Our students’ mastery will compound and accelerate over four years and put them at an advantage when it comes to pursuing STEM careers.” The shift also opens the pathways for all students to take AP Calculus by their junior or senior year. something less than 10 percent of students were previously able to achieve. “We’re giving students a rock-solid foundation to excel in Pre Calculus, Finite Math, Data Science or even AP Calculus as juniors,” Trujillo emphasized. There are a range of AP courses they can take, even Multivariable Calculus. “O’Dowd is one of only a few high schools in the nation that teaches this,” Trujillo said. Multivariable Calculus lays the mathematical foundation for machine learning and theoretical computer science. “We need to be preparing students to be drivers and innovators of the kinds of systems that Google Maps and Spotify are built on,” Trujillo insists. “They’re going to keep changing the world.” J.D. Childs is President of Bishop O’Dowd High School.

Competing in the prestigious 9th annual MLK Showcase, a collection of 24 top ranked teams hosted by St. Mary’s in Stockton, Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team came up big with a convincing 60-43 win against Los Angeles power Lynwood on Saturday, January 15. “Overall, it was a great game. Everybody contributed with effort and toughness, and that’s what you want to see,” said Piedmont coach Bryan Gardere. “We’re playing well and will try to keep that competitive greatness at a high level. We played really tough defense and shut them down going into halftime.” Natalie Martinez had a 14-point outburst in the second quarter, and led her team with 25 points and nine rebounds. Trinity Zamora had a double-double with 21 points and 14 rebounds. PHS jumped out to a commanding 18-11 lead in the first quarter, then turned its vaunted defense loose to hold Lynwood to only three points before halftime. The Highlanders extended the lead to 45-27 in the third and finished out strong at 60-43. In the first quarter, Zamora scored six points on 3-pointers, while forward Kat Melian, a sophomore and first-year varsity starter, had four points and several key rebounds. “Kat Melian is having a good year. She is really tough and always shows high-effort,” said Gardere. Zamora added six more points in the second quarter, and Maddie Hill added five points with a 3-pointer and a pair of free throws. “Maddie is a great leader for us. She had some fantastic on-ball defense,” said Gardere. After halftime it was the Natalie Martinez show. The Trinity Zamora had a double-double with 21 points and 14 rebounds. Gardere had high praise for Maddie Hill’s on-ball defense in the MLK Showcase.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team’s defense led the way to a gritty 2-1 victory over Castro Valley on the road on Friday, January 14, on goals by Rachel Barton and Nina Goldberg. The Trojans controlled ball possession for most of the game, and had opportunities to score on 12 corner kicks, but the PHS defense held strong. “I would say we were the stronger team in the first half, while in the second we were definitely under pressure. They had a ton of [chances], but they didn’t create much to threaten the goal,” said Piedmont coach Dan Chubbock. “They hit us a lot on the counter attack, but [our] girls looked like they were having fun out there.” Rachel Barton scored in the seventh minute to put Piedmont in front, 1-0. Castro Valley tied the match shortly after halftime in the 37th minute. The Trojans’ joy was short-lived when PHS captain Nina Goldberg scored two minutes later on a nifty header assisted by Emily Fitzgerald. Barton has been a standout winger in Piedmont’s attack throughout the season, often maintaining possession against tight defense to create scoring chances. “We have a really solid front line,” said Barton. “Emily is so good at getting those passes down to me. A lot of it is the communication on getting the ball down the field and me booking to try and get it. This year, I’ve worked really hard on crossing and getting my hips around the ball to really angle the ball in front of the goalie.” Making an enormous difference in Thursday’s match was Audrey Lam, Piedmont’s maestro in the midfield. She was instrumental in controlling the ball, creating scoring chances with slick footwork, and tracking back to help out on defense. “Audrey’s work rate getting back and forth is amazing. She had a defensive header that reminded me of LeBron James in the 2016 NBA Finals. She wanted to win this game, it was fun to watch her,” said coach Chubbock. Match Recap The action got off to a fast start with Piedmont’s first shot on goal coming in the third minute. The goal by Barton came after Goldberg sent a long ball to Fitzgerald, who sent a through ball down the right side to Barton. Staff Photos Emily Fitzgerald (left) and Tucker Donahue (right) celebrate with Rachel Barton (15) after Barton’s goal against Castro Valley. Emily Fitzgerald assisted on both Piedmont goals against Castro Valley. Her right-footed shot curled over the Trojans’ keeper to the far post for the goal and a 1-0 lead 7 minutes into the game. CV had a couple of near chances in the following minutes, including a shot going over the net in the ninth minute and another shot skirt wide in the 11th. Castro Valley’s goal came in the 37th minute after goalkeeper Morgan Hunt tried to crash on an approaching forward, who chipped the ball over Hunt into the net. But two minutes later, only one minute before halftime, Piedmont recaptured the lead on a corner kick into the penalty area. The ball skipped toward Fitzgerald, who instinctively volleyed a header back toward Goldberg, who slotted in the goal to make it 2-1. In the second half, Castro Valley controlled the action and opened the first 18 minutes of the final 40 with one shot on target and four corners. Hunt, meanwhile, had a critical diving save in the 71st minute to maintain Piedmont’s tenuous lead. CV had another shot on goal go wide in the 74th and another long shot easily saved in the 76th. By Jonathan Comeaux Competing in the prestigious 9th annual MLK Showcase, a collection of 24 top ranked teams hosted by St. Mary’s in Stockton, Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team came up big with a convincing 60-43 win against Los Angeles power Lynwood on Saturday, January 15. “Overall, it was a great game. We played really tough defense and shut them down going into halftime.” Natalie Martinez had a 14-point outburst in the second quarter, and led her team with 25 points and nine rebounds. Trinity Zamora had a double-double with 21 points and 14 rebounds. PHS jumped out to a commanding 18-11 lead in the first quarter, then turned its vaunted defense loose to hold Lynwood to only three points before halftime. The Highlanders extended the lead to 45-27 in the third and finished out strong at 60-43. In the first quarter, Zamora scored six points on 3-pointers, while forward Kat Melian, a sophomore and first-year varsity starter, had four points and several key rebounds. “Kat Melian is having a good year. articles.text: Come see Golden Gate Park’s Peacock Meadow as it is transformed into an enchanted forest of otherworldly shapes and ever-changing light. “Entwined,” a public art installation by San Francisco artist Charles Gadeken, creates a whimsical wonderland where visitors can explore paths and sit under a grove of three entwined sculptural trees. A public art installation, “Entwined” is currently located adjacent to the Conservatory of Flowers in Golden Gate Park. “Entwined” by Charles Gadeken Gadeken is an industrial artist who for over 25 years has created monumental interactive public artworks that reimagine the world “post-nature.” His work has been commissioned by Black Rock Arts Foundation, City of San Francisco, Insomniac Events, Coachella, Absolut Vodka, City of Palo Alto, City of Calabasas, City of Los Altos, and Stanford University. Many of his works have been exhibited internationally. “Entwined” is available to view from dusk until 8:30 p.m. Those who visit are asked to wear a mask at all times and practice social distancing. Viewing is free and tickets are not required.
articles.title: Visit “Entwined” in Golden Gate Park now through February 1

articles.text: Celebrate Lunar New Year at Oakland Museum with programs highlighting the Year of the Tiger. Oakland Museum of California is celebrating the Year of the Tiger with a series of Lunar New Year programs beginning January 25. A mix of online and in-person activities will be offered as part of the museum’s 21st Annual Lunar New Year Celebration. This year’s events celebrate the range of Asian cultures and traditions that make up the Oakland community, and display the strength, bravery, and resilience of the Tiger. The festivities will begin on Tuesday, January 25, with a virtual cooking demonstration by OMCA staff member Linda Jia. Jia will demonstrate how to make dumplings, a traditional Lunar New Year dish. You can watch the demonstration on the museum’s YouTube channel by visiting https://www. youtube.com/watch?v=BGhBNZfrS1s. February 1 Families will enjoy a virtual, hands-on shadow puppet art activity on Tuesday, February 1 led by museum staff member Leslie Cheng. She will show audiences how to make shadow puppets, an ancient form of storytelling. Shadow puppet kits can be downloaded from the museum’s website. February 5 On February 5, audiences are invited to visit the museum and participate in story time with famed San Francisco author Oliver Chin. Chin recently launched a new graphic novel series entitled Awesome Asian Americans. A limited capacity, family-friendly in-person celebration will be held at the museum on Saturday, February 5 from 12 p.m. to 3 p.m. Proof of vaccination will be required to attend. For a full schedule of events, visit https://museumca.org/lunarnew-year-celebration-year-tiger.
articles.title: Oakland Museum announces plans to celebrate Lunar New Year

articles.text: For mer Music Director Michael Tilson Thomas (MTT) will conduct the San Francisco Symphony in two weeks of concerts live at Davies Symphony Hall. The first concerts, held January 20 through 22, will include Sergei Prokofiev’s Symphony No. 5 and Dmitri Shostakovich’s Cello Concerto No. 2 performed by cellist Gautier Capucon. The second series, January 27 through 29, will include Gustav Mahler’s Symphony No. 1 – a staple in Tilson Thomas’ repertoire – and pianist Yuja Wang performing Franz Liszt’s Piano Concerto No. 1. MTT became Music Director of the San Francisco Symphony in 1995, and for 25 years led the symphony in championing contemporary and American composers alongside classical masters. Though retired, he continues to lead the orchestra in four weeks of concerts annually. Tickets for concerts at Davies Symphony Hall may be purchased at www.sfsymphony. org, or by calling the box office at (415) 864-6000. articles.text: Sa n Fr a nci s c o Ba l le t announced the appointment of Tamara Rojo as Artistic Director on January 11. She is the first woman to lead the ballet company and will succeed Helgi Tomasson, who led the company for nearly 40 years, and retires in June this year. articles.text: Emily Blunt stars in The Girl on the Train. Earlier this year I picked up Paula Hawkins’ novel, The Girl on the Train. Written in 2015, it reached the bestseller list and was often compared to Gillian Flynn’s novel Gone Girl, also a mystery-thriller that included multiple points of view. I confess that I read most of Hawkins’ book and then stopped, something I rarely do. Usually, I’ll power through a book despite whatever flaws tempt me to put it down. Caveat phrase: “So little time, so many books.” What caused me to stop reading The Girl on the Train was its unreliable narrator, Ruth Watson. She continually made awful choices, many while in a drunken stupor. I simply came to a point where I didn’t want to spend any more time with her. I share all this to say that I was, therefore, hesitant to see the film. But I know Emily Blunt, who portrays Rachel, to be a gifted actor and was curious how she would interpret the character. decided that Blunt’s portrayal, while maddening at times, was spot on. Though the story is about three women and their points of view, it is Blunt who is the hub of the wagon wheel, so to speak. I am reluctant to share too much of the plot in this review because Girl is a mystery-thriller of a sort, one in which pieces of a puzzle are scattered in front of the audience, using multiple flashbacks, with real-time segments showing Rachel taking a commuter train into Manhattan from Westchester and then returning. While she rides, she sips constantly from a water bottle filled with vodka and all that she sees is seen through a prism distorted by alcohol. What is real and what is fantasy is, at least to her, unknowable. She often spots a couple standing on their second story porch in an embrace, and begins looking for them, willing herself not to look while nurturing the idea that they share a perfect love. With each brief glimpse, as the train passes by, she observes them closely understanding that their companionship wounds her and yet enthralls her. Compounding her pain and fascination is the fact that the house of this anonymous couple is just three doors away from a home that she once shared with her now ex-husband, Tom (Justin Theroux), who lives there with his new wife, Anna (Rebecca Ferguson) and their new baby. He is now living the life she so desperately wanted to share with him. Rachel is a fantasist, damaged and chronically self- destructive. One late afternoon she spots from the train the woman (Haley Bennett) standing on the familiar porch, but she is in the arms of a different man. Rachel reacts with rage, feeling she has personally been betrayed. And then the woman, Megan, goes missing. And so the narrative continues as Rachel staggers into the life of Megan’s husband, Scott (Luke Evans). She tries to reconstruct her connection to Megan, knowing they were strangers yet is certain she knows something about why she has gone missing. But the shroud of alcohol makes any attempt at full recall elusive. The pieces of the puzzle are scattered, and it is up to the audience to fit them together with little help from Rachel who binges into deeper dysfunction. What is also revealed is that Megan and Anna are not who they appear to be either. Especially Megan. This is a film with many twists. I was curious to see how Hawkins would bring all the disparate parts together, and I wasn’t disappointed. As an aside, the cast is remarkable. Emily Blunt’s performance is worthy of an award for best actress. The Girl on the Train. Directed by Tate Taylor. Starring Emily Blunt, Haley Bennett, Justin Theroux. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated R.

Mussolini‘s son turned out to be a famous jazz pianist, who was respected on his own. Former U.S. President Harry Truman practiced the piano every day, and was a supporter of the arts.

articles.text: Disney began its remarkable history of animated stories with a singular mouse, Mickey. So, it’s no surprise that once again the animators have returned to The Great Mouse Detective, based on the children’s book series, Basil of Baker Street, by Eve Titus and Paul Galone. The writers embraced the still budding technology of CGI, realizing that the contemporary audience of kids wanted something a bit more zany. Anthropomorphism alone doesn’t quite cut it. The result is Detective, with a compelling cast of mice and rats, all living in Victorian England in 1897. The tale begins by introducing Olivia Flaversham (Susanne Pollatscheck) and her father Hiram (Alan Young), a master toymaker. Unexpectedly, Hiram, while working in his shop, is kidnapped by a strange bat called Fidget (Candy Candido). He’s a malevolent creature with a broken wing and a peg leg, and bursts in and snatches Olivia’s father. She is at first frantic and at loss as what to do; but then sets out to find the famed mouse detective, Basil of Baker Street (Barrie Ingham), who actually lives in the foundation of the home of Sherlock Homes. When Basil learns that the rogue kidnapper was Fidget, the henchman of his nemesis, Professor Ratigan (Vincent Price), a villain he has pursued for years, he immediately takes the case and sets out to solve the mystery of the missing Hiram. And so the hunt begins, a story filled with schemes by Ratigan, whose ultimate dream is to become the supreme ruler of all of England’s Mousedom. The search even includes Sherlock Holmes’ own Basset Hound, Toby (Frank Welker). The plot is exciting, and involves Olivia being kidnapped, a massive dirigible owned by Ratigan who intends to use it to make last minute escapes. He even manages to crash into the Big Ben tower clock, where, as it turns out, Olivia is being held captive. Kids will enjoy The Great Mouse Detective from the get go. There is not only a mystery to be solved, but offers nonstop action, led by Basil, magnifying glass in hand (naturally), who is in hot pursuit of the villainous Ratigan. At his side, of course, is his trusty assistant Dawson (Van Bettin). The Great Mouse Detective. Disney Animation. Directed by John Musker. 1 hr., 20 min. Rated G. articles.text: Film review by Chris Honoré Benji (2018) is a remake of the popular 1974 family-friendly film that focuses on the love of a stray dog by two latchkey kids, Carter and Frankie Hughes (Gabriel Bateman and Darby Camp) who recently lost their father, and live with their single mom, Whitney Hughes (Kiele Sanchez). The story opens when a mother canine and her small litter are taken to the animal shelter by a malevolent dogcatcher. Out of the shadows appears the face of a pint-sized pooch, watching as the family is carted off. He is a mixed-breed dog who lives on the street, searching for food wherever he can find it. In his travels, he meets up with Carter and Frankie. They try and feed him some strawberries, but he is cautious and timid; however, he quickly realizes that the kids will not hurt him and follows them home. Carter spots the little guy outside, and they decide to bring him inside, though uncertain of their mom’s reaction, and hide him under a pile of stuffed animals. Frankie wants to name him after Benjamin Franklin, which naturally gets shortened to Benji. When Whitney discovers Benji, she insists that the kids take the stray back where they found him. With regret they obey, and leaving Benji to fend for himself they stop off at Mr. Sam’s Pawn Shop (Gralen Bryant Banks). Without their knowing, Benji follows them. To their surprise, they walk into the middle of a robbery carried out by two thugs (Will Rothhaar and Angus Sampson). When one of their masks slips off, they realize that Carter and Frankie can identify them and so they kidnap the kids, forcing them into a van. Benji, who has been outside waiting, sees this taking place and chases after the van, all the way to the robbers’ hideout, a large, decaying plantation house. Watching the kids being taken into the house, and seeing that the men own a mean-looking Rottweiler, Benji hurries back to Grant and Frankie’s home where he tries to convince Whitney and a friendly cop, Lyle (Jerod Haynes), to follow him back to the hideout. Of course, the children in the audience are rooting for Benji, and hoping that the adults will figure out what Benji is trying to say. But Benji never utters a word, and the filmmakers never use voiceover or CGI lip movement. All that Benji urgently wants to say must be conveyed by his facial expressions. This is known as the Kuleshov method: the audience attributes emotions and communication to what is essentially a blank face, which, in this case, belongs to Benji. There are harrowing moments, chases, and the challenge to outwit the bad guys in order to rescue the kids. The children in the audience will be riveted to their seats, and definitely will fall in love with Benji. Benji. Written and directed by Brandon Camp. Streaming on Netflix. Starring Gabriel Bateman, Darby Camp, Kiele Sanchez. 1 hr., 6 min. Rated G.

articles.text: What is fun? One definition is enjoyment, amusement, or lighthearted pleasure. Piedmont Scouts in Troop 11 got to experience many exciting and engaging things on a recent trip to Dillon Beach on the Sonoma coast that topped the definition of fun. As a new Scout I was blown away by the experience and activities presented for us. I especially enjoyed the sand dunes, where we spent several hours exploring. One memorable moment was launching model rockets. They blasted off into the sky so fast just like the concept of time. In addition, troop members brought bobsleds and we all took turns sliding down the huge dunes. We also buried some members in the thick sand, and some of us even lost our shoes in the endless dunes. When looking into the distance, it was like there was no end. I had a wonderful time playing hide-and-go-seek with my friends as we ran across the deep dunes, smelling sand. It was truly magical. In Scouting, we learn to take responsibility for ourselves, and learn the power of leadership. We had a great opportunity demonstrating our leadership skills in the Troop cooking competition where each Patrol was tasked to make a main dish on a budget. The dish had to include a vegetable and carb balance. Some of the dishes included spaghetti and meatballs, tacos, pizza, and steak. All of the dishes were amazing, but the Mildewed Mangoes Patrol took first place and won the Golden Spatula. The Gremlins Patrol lost by only 1/10 of a point and took second. As part of the Gremlins Patrol, I enjoyed working with my peers to create a delicious dish. The Gremlins made spaghetti and meatballs along with an improvised salad. We all had a chance to go to the beach and see the big sea lions. They were vast like the moon, and their poise was mystical. The next morning each Patrol made their own breakfast. We even had a chance to try some fresh crab that had been caught that morning. The crab was shared amongst the whole troop, and it was delicious. Afterwards some Scouts participated in a beach cleanup, while others stayed back to learn about knife and ax tools and how to build a fire. The beach cleanup group was happy to report there was not as much trash as expected. Although it was quite windy, Troop 11 Scouts learn to fish for crab from the beach. the Scouts learned to build bonfires and got some good flames – at least for a little while. Troop 11 ended its fantastic journey with a closing circle and talking about the roses and thorns of the trip. Everyone described the thrill they had on the sand dunes. And although it was a cold trip, we had a very memorable time with our friends, whether wrestling over shoes, arm wrestling, or watching cheesy skits. articles.text: Sadly, identity theft happens throughout the year – but some identity thieves are particularly active during tax-filing season. How can you protect yourself? One of the most important moves you can make is to be suspicious of requests by people or entities claiming to be from the Internal Revenue Service. You may receive phone calls, texts and emails, but these types of communication are often just “phishing” scams with one goal in mind: to capture your personal information. These phishers can be quite clever, sending emails that appear to contain the IRS logo or making calls that may even seem to be coming from the IRS. Don’t open any links or attachments to the emails and don’t answer the calls – and don’t be alarmed if the caller leaves a vaguely threatening voicemail, either asking for personal information, such as your Social Security number, or informing you of some debts you supposedly owe to the IRS that must be taken care of “immediately.” In reality, the IRS will not initiate contact with you by phone, email, text message or social media to request personal or financial information, or to inquire about issues pertaining to your tax returns. Instead, the agency will first send you a letter. And if you’re unsure of the legitimacy of such a letter, contact the IRS directly at 800-829-1040. Of course, not all scam artists are fake IRS representatives – some will pass themselves off as tax preparers. Fortunately, most tax preparers are honest, but it’s not too hard to find the dishonest ones who might ask you to sign a blank return, promise you a big refund before looking at your records or try to charge a fee based on the percentage of your return. Legitimate tax preparers will make no grand promises and will explain their fees upfront. Before hiring someone to do your taxes, find out their qualifications. The IRS provides some valuable tips for choosing a reputable tax preparer, but you can also ask your friends and relatives for referrals. Another tax scam to watch out for is the fraudulent tax return – that is, someone filing a return in your name. To do so, a scammer would need your name, birthdate and Social Security number. If you’re already providing two of these pieces of information – your name and birthdate on social media, and you also include your birthplace – you could be making it easier for scam artists to somehow get the third. It’s a good idea to check your privacy settings and limit what you’re sharing publicly. You might also want to use a nickname and omit your last name, birthday and birthplace. Here’s one more defensive measure: File your taxes as soon as you can. Identity thieves often strike early in the tax season, so they can file their bogus returns before their victims. To learn more about tax scams, visit the IRS website (irs.gov) and search for the “Taxpayer Guide to Identity Theft.” This document describes some signs of identity theft and provides tips for what to do if you are victimized. It’s unfortunate that identity theft exists, but by taking the proper precautions, you can help insulate yourself from this threat, even when tax season is over. Pictured are: Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Jim Kellogg, Ken Young, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Wenny Young, Christine Calliste, Priscilla Wanerus, Dena Belinkoff, Quincy Dong, Kat Lang, Aaron Katzel, Helen Dong, Pat Keller, Siow Fang Tan, Lilly Guardia-Labar, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Bob Gustafson, Nadine Guffanti, Stella Houston, Sarah Johnson, Jim Kuo, Melba Yee, Phil Witte, Alicia Rivera, and Dick Carter. The group welcomed Peter Persoff back for his first walk since the pandemic hiatus. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group enjoys learning about Piedmont’s history and also how it relates to the streets they walk. At the start of a New Year it seemed appropriate that the walk on January 12 would have a focus on the early period of the region’s history. So, it was decided that this walk would be about Walter Blair, for whom Blair Avenue is named. A strong showing of 28 walkers and one K-9 best friend were at the Exedra on this sunny, winter morning. Drawing on the research of Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi, the history of Blair was shared with the group. His parents were Vermont farmers of Scottish descent, and he was one of 12 children. He came to California in 1852 during the gold rush and at age 22 he became the first European settler in the Piedmont hills. He was a dairy farmer, capitalist, and founder of the original Blair Park. In 1852 Blair purchased 600 acres in the Piedmont hills for $750. It encompassed most of the land between today’s Moraga, Scenic, Magnolia and Grand Avenues. Blair’s original cabin was where the modern home at 111 Highland Avenue is now located. Blair called his street “Vernal Avenue” because of its lush ferns and shrubs. The back of the house was on today’s Waldo Avenue. The walkers headed off on Highland (not Vernal) Avenue, noting historic homes as they went. They continued to the end of Highland at Moraga Avenue. They looked across the street to the spot where an arched entrance to Blair Park once stood, and more of Blair’s history was told. Blair established Blair’s Dairy at the corner of today’s Blair and El Cerrito Avenues, and his cattle grazed in pastures that went down to what is now Grand Avenue. However, he found real estate and other commercial interests to be also profitable. He built the Piedmont Springs Hotel in 1871, which was at the top of today’s Piedmont Park, and partnered with investors to build a horsecar line from downtown Oakland to Piedmont Avenue. In 1878 Blair decided to build his own line, the Piedmont Railway, which ran from where the Piedmont Avenue line ended at the gates of the Mountain View Cemetery, and went through his grain fields to Vernal Avenue and the Piedmont Springs Hotel. To increase the number of riders, in 1884 Blair developed 40 acres of the land between the cemetery and Moraga Avenue as a picnic park, and named it Blair Park. It offered picnic tables, paths for wandering, a Japanese Tea House, a dancing pavilion, a Venetian canal ride, a bandstand, swings, bridges over waterfalls and a stream, a fountain, a lake, and even hot air balloon ascensions. Many of the picnickers and hotel guests enjoyed the views and climate in Piedmont and stayed to purchase property and build homes. They became Piedmont’s early residents. Blair also opened the Dracena Quarry, which is today’s Dracena Park, to sell crushed rock to pave the streets of Oakland, Piedmont and the nearby Mountain View Cemetery. Blair was only 57 when he died in 1888. He is buried in Mountain View Cemetery. After his death Blair Park was purchased by another train line, but it went into receivership in 1893, and its assets were sold in 1895. In 1901 the park was abandoned, and the land was still vacant in 1913, but in 1917 new homes began to be built on it. A builder, Guy Turner, constructed 11 bungalows on the cemetery side of Moraga Avenue and at least six more a few years later. The walkers made their way down Moraga looking at the homes that Turner built 100 years ago. At the end of the long wall marks the property of Mountain View Cemetery, the group crossed Moraga Avenue and, for the first time, walked the oneway, seldom-traveled, Oakland portion of Ramona Avenue. On the right side of the street was a small house with a full cactus garden that covered the entire front yard. At the street’s end was the spot on Piedmont Avenue, just down from the entrance to the cemetery, where Blair’s trolley cars started their climb up to Vernal Avenue. The walkers also looked across the street and admired the historic Julia Morgan-designed Chapel of the Chimes and mausoleum. On the way back to Pleasant Valley Road, Pat Keller and some other walkers knew of a set of three hidden paths that cut across the horseshoe-shaped North and South Pleasant Valley Court to Moraga Avenue. The group walked the paths and down the seldom-walked Parkside Drive cul-de-sac. Then it was on to Arroyo and Lower Grand Avenues, Holly Place, and a path on York Drive that took them to Ricardo Avenue at the foot of Dracena Park, the site of Blair’s quarry. The last leg of the return to the Exedra started with the steep 100 block of El Cerrito Avenue to its intersection with Blair Avenue, the site of Blair’s dairy. The walk was completed with a hike up Blair Avenue, through what was once his gain fields, past the back of his home on Waldo Avenue, and then down Highland Avenue to the Exedra, where Blair’s Piedmont Springs Hotel once stood. The group finished the 3-1/2 mile Walter Blair historical tour in 90 minutes. As they returned to the Exedra they had a better understanding and appreciation of the lasting impact Walter Blair made on the city of Piedmont. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday, rain or shine, at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: Civilizations around the world have been celebrating the start of each New Year for at least 4,000 years. Common traditions include attending parties, eating special New Year’s food, making resolutions for the new year and watching fireworks displays. But when the singing, fireworks and champagne toasts are over, many of us become more serious about life. We take stock and plan new courses of action to better our lives. This is best seen in one of the most popular customs of the new year, making resolutions. So why are so many of my friends shunning this custom this year? I was having a discussion about making resolutions with a group of Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living residents the other day. Our residents have had the chance to make many resolutions for each of their new years. After my informal poll, the general consensus was to not make resolutions. Pat said, “In all honesty, I don’t make them, because I never can keep them!” Gloria added, “New Year’s Day is a new chance to try again. Yet, I don’t make resolutions, because each and every day I look forward to doing better!” Another resident added, “I think of each day as a new beginning.” Since many resolutions result in taking something away, I think I will adopt Gloria’s approach. It seems one is more likely to accomplish a goal that is specific and based on doing something each day instead of avoiding Lake Merritt resident Laura McGee considers her New Year’s resolutions. something or taking something away. I always appreciate talking with our residents. There is definitely something to be learned from aging and wisdom. As I’ve travelled through life, I have learned that it’s better for me not to make a New Year’s resolution, than to make one and fail. So my goal to cut down on sugar will result in my buying only one box of cookies from the grocery store each week. My main goal, to resume my exercise regime, will begin after my birthday celebration - which is just around the corner. Our residents seem to be in agreement that the time to set goals is when we are motivated to keep them, not just because the calendar is turned to a new page. I think that with this approach we have a better chance at keeping our resolutions rather than having failure again slap us in the face. Let’s set and keep goals, not just at the New Year, but at any time we feel moved to do so. Welcome 2022. We have the entire year of fresh starts ahead of us. Happy New Year! Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living at 1800 Madison Street in Oakland. Call 510-903-3600 or visit www. thelakemerritt.com.

articles.text: Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I just got a new MacBook Air that is still in the box. I am trying to decide if I should transfer all of my files with Time Machine or just start fresh? I have years of stuff that I don’t use, and I started to have some trouble opening some of my files. Also, some of my applications (on my old laptop) have been shutting down unexpectedly. All I really do these days is use my email, write a few Word files, and take photos. My email is through Gmail. The salesperson at Best Buy suggested that I use Dropbox or iCloud to store and transfer my files. Can you explain how that would be different than transferring everything with Time Machine? –Lissa M., Oakland Dear Lissa: This is a great question. It’s your second sentence that leads me to my answer. Since you are having some application crashes and also have a ton of old files you don’t need, I would recommend setting this up as a new machine. That being said, it would also be possible and even desirable to use Dropbox or iCloud to transfer the files you do want. If you only have a few files that you want to keep, and by “a few” I mean less than a gigabyte or so, I would recommend moving them to a folder in Dropbox before you set up your new Mac. Dropbox is a cloud service. You can think of it as a virtual hard drive. You must have an account, and most likely if you’re going to use it to sync files you already have on your computer, you’re going to want one of their paid accounts. You download the application, sign into your account, and then you would have a folder in finder called, “Dropbox”. Anything that you move into Dropbox; folders, files, pictures, etc. can be synced with other machines that are signed into the same Dropbox account. This gives you the most control over what you want to move over to the new machine. You could create a folder on the desktop of your old machine, called something like “To Be Transferred” or “Keepers”. Then you would simply upload that folder to Dropbox, which is as simple as dragging to the Dropbox icon in Finder. There are plenty of tutorials online about using this application, and their website, www.dropbox.com has very good ones. The nice thing about this is that you can cherry pick things to move over. If you use iCloud to sync your desktop and documents, it will sync everything on your desktop and documents. Anything you don’t want to be stored in iCloud, you have to move out of your documents folder and off of your desktop. This system is great if you want everything to look the same on more than one machine, but not practical if you only want to move a few files over. In your situation, I think Dropbox makes more sense. As far as your photos go, if you haven’t already, I would enable iCloud Photos to sync on your laptop as well as your phone before you set up the new machine. This way, when you sign into iCloud on your new Air, and enable iCloud Photos, all of your photos will come into your photo library. If you have tens of thousands of photos, then make sure to do this well enough ahead of time that the complete library has a chance to upload to iCloud. Since you use Gmail, when you set your email up on the new machine, everything that’s on Gmail’s servers will come into your mail application, so that’s no problem. What won’t come over are any emails you are saving locally; that means folders stored under “On my Mac” in Apple Mail. If this is the case, re-create these folders under Gmail in the folders list in Mac mail, and copy any of the emails in the local folders to Gmail ones. Again, there are lots of tutorials online about how to do this. Here is what makes all of this different than using your Time Machine back up drive to transfer your data. When you use Time Machine, it copies everything on your current computer every hour onto an external drive. This includes everything you see, like documents, files, folders, pictures, your music and photo library, all of your applications, as well as things you don’t see, like preferences, drivers, and files that live in the user and system library. So, if one or more of those files are corrupt, Time Machine still copies it. If you migrate these files to a new computer, it is possible you will inherit any problems you had on your old machine. For this reason, in your case, I would recommend the Dropbox solution. Personally, I use a combination of iCloud and Dropbox. And of course, if you need help, you can contact me, and I can help with the new set up. This article first appeared in the Post on March 31, 2021. Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com and themacmama.blogspot.com.

articles.text: There are many reasons that someone becomes a caregiver: they have been caring for a family member and discovered their strengths in being compassionate; they are following a path into nursing or related medical field and want some hands-on experience; or they enjoy helping others and developing meaningful oneon-one connections. As caregiving becomes a high in-demand career with more people living longer in the comfort of their own homes, there can also be financial incentives to consider this job. The need for quality caregivers has possibly never been greater. Yet there are reasons that caregiving can be more than just a job. We’d like to share five of them: 1. Transferable skills The skills gained in a caregiving job can apply to all kinds of other roles, including some in the home care agency office. Things like being compassionate, being a good listener, showing patience, and other qualities used to assist people whose abilities have changed due to illness or age can be used in all other personal and professional situations to your benefit. 2. Training At Homewatch CareGivers, caregivers have the opportunity for additional training via the Homewatch CareGivers University which can empower them to grow professionally. These courses may include dementia care, behavioral health, instructions on caring for people who are living with intellectual and developmental disabilities, and much more. Once you start learning, there is no telling how far you can go in a career. 3. Flexibility Caregivers often have scheduling flexibility, much different than a traditional 9 to 5 type of job, which means they have the ability to pick and choose what suits them and their own families while earning money from their career. 4. Making a difference Yes, a smile can change someone’s world. Many people who need in-home care services have become isolated from a life that brought them joy. Symptoms of chronic conditions may limit their abilities to engage in certain activities or socialize as they once did. A friendly caregiver who provides transportation for errands, plays a fun board game, gives medication reminders, and much more, can alleviate their feelings of loneliness, helplessness, and boredom. 5. Each day is new. Caregiving may have challenges and surprises and that can help you to grow personally and professionally, as well as bring laughs and new life skills. Each client is unique and brings their own life story and needs to the relationship, and a chance to learn more. This is best seen in one of the most popular customs of the new year, making resolutions. So why are so many of my friends shunning this custom this year? I was having a discussion about making resolutions with a group of Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living residents the other day. Our residents have had the chance to make many resolutions for each of their new years. After my informal poll, the general consensus was to not make resolutions. Pat said, “In all honesty, I don’t make them, because I never can keep them!” Gloria added, “New Year’s Day is a new chance to try again. Yet, I don’t make resolutions, because each and every day I look forward to doing better!” Another resident added, “I think of each day as a new beginning.” Since many resolutions result in taking something away, I think I will adopt Gloria’s approach. It seems one is more likely to accomplish a goal that is specific and based on doing something each day instead of avoiding Lake Merritt resident Laura McGee considers her New Year’s resolutions. something or taking something away. I always appreciate talking with our residents. There is definitely something to be learned from aging and wisdom. As I’ve travelled through life, I have learned that it’s better for me not to make a New Year’s resolution, than to make one and fail. So my goal to cut down on sugar will result in my buying only one box of cookies from the grocery store each week. My main goal, to resume my exercise regime, will begin after my birthday celebration - which is just around the corner. Our residents seem to be in agreement that the time to set goals is when we are motivated to keep them, not just because the calendar is turned to a new page. I think that with this approach we have a better chance at keeping our resolutions rather than having failure again slap us in the face. Let’s set and keep goals, not just at the New Year, but at any time we feel moved to do so. Welcome 2022. We have the entire year of fresh starts ahead of us. Happy New Year! As caregiving becomes a high in-demand career with more people living longer in the comfort of their own homes, there can also be financial incentives to consider this job. The need for quality caregivers has possibly never been greater. Yet there are reasons that caregiving can be more than just a job. We’d like to share five of them: 1. Transferable skills The skills gained in a caregiving job can apply to all kinds of other roles, including some in the home care agency office. Things like being compassionate, being a good listener, showing patience, and other qualities used to assist people whose abilities have changed due to illness or age can be used in all other personal and professional situations to your benefit. 2. Training At Homewatch CareGivers, caregivers have the opportunity for additional training via the Homewatch CareGivers University which can empower them to grow professionally. These courses may include dementia care, behavioral health, instructions on caring for people who are living with intellectual and developmental disabilities, and much more. Once you start learning, there is no telling how far you can go in a career. 3. Flexibility Caregivers often have scheduling flexibility, much different than a traditional 9 to 5 type of job, which means they have the ability to pick and choose what suits them and their own families while earning money from their career. 4. Making a difference Yes, a smile can change someone’s world. Many people who need in-home care services have become isolated from a life that brought them joy. Symptoms of chronic conditions may limit their abilities to engage in certain activities or socialize as they once did. A friendly caregiver who provides transportation for errands, plays a fun board game, gives medication reminders, and much more, can alleviate their feelings of loneliness, helplessness, and boredom. 5. Each day is new. Caregiving may have challenges and surprises and that can help you to grow personally and professionally, as well as bring laughs and new life skills. Each client is unique and brings their own life story and needs to the relationship, and a chance to learn more. The advantages of using Time Machine for files By Cookie Segelstein Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I just got a new MacBook Air that is still in the box. I am trying to decide if I should transfer all of my files with Time Machine or just start fresh? I have years of stuff that I don’t use, and I started to have some trouble opening some of my files. Also, some of my applications (on my old laptop) have been shutting down unexpectedly. All I really do these days is use my email, write a few Word files, and take photos. My email is through Gmail. The salesperson at Best Buy suggested that I use Dropbox or iCloud to store and transfer my files. Can you explain how that would be different than transferring everything with Time Machine? –Lissa M., Oakland Dear Lissa: This is a great question. It’s your second sentence that leads me to my answer. Since you are having some application crashes and also have a ton of old files you don’t need, I would recommend setting this up as a new machine. That being said, it would also be possible and even desirable to use Dropbox or iCloud to transfer the files you do want. If you only have a few files that you want to keep, and by “a few” I mean less than a gigabyte or so, I would recommend moving them to a folder in Dropbox before you set up your new Mac. Dropbox is a cloud service. You can think of it as a virtual hard drive. You must have an account, and most likely if you’re going to use it to sync files you already have on your computer, you’re going to want one of their paid accounts. You download the application, sign into your account, and then you would have a folder in finder called, “Dropbox”. Anything that you move into Dropbox; folders, files, pictures, etc. can be synced with other machines that are signed into the same Dropbox account. This gives you the most control over what you want to move over to the new machine. You could create a folder on the desktop of your old machine, called something like “To Be Transferred” or “Keepers”. Then you would simply upload that folder to Dropbox, which is as simple as dragging to the Dropbox icon in Finder. There are plenty of tutorials online about using this application, and their website, www.dropbox.com has very good ones. The nice thing about this is that you can cherry pick things to move over. If you use iCloud to sync your desktop and documents, it will sync everything on your desktop and documents. Anything you don’t want to be stored in iCloud, you have to move out of your documents folder and off of your desktop. This system is great if you want everything to look the same on more than one machine, but not practical if you only want to move a few files over. In your situation, I think Dropbox makes more sense. As far as your photos go, if you haven’t already, I would enable iCloud Photos to sync on your laptop as well as your phone before you set up the new machine. This way, when you sign into iCloud on your new Air, and enable iCloud Photos, all of your photos will come into your photo library. If you have tens of thousands of photos, then make sure to do this well enough ahead of time that the complete library has a chance to upload to iCloud. Since you use Gmail, when you set your email up on the new machine, everything that’s on Gmail’s servers will come into your mail application, so that’s no problem. What won’t come over are any emails you are saving locally; that means folders stored under “On my Mac” in Apple Mail. If this is the case, re-create these folders under Gmail in the folders list in Mac mail, and copy any of the emails in the local folders to Gmail ones. Again, there are lots of tutorials online about how to do this. Here is what makes all of this different than using your Time Machine back up drive to transfer your data. When you use Time Machine, it copies everything on your current computer every hour onto an external drive. This includes everything you see, like documents, files, folders, pictures, your music and photo library, all of your applications, as well as things you don’t see, like preferences, drivers, and files that live in the user and system library. So, if one or more of those files are corrupt, Time Machine still copies it. If you migrate these files to a new computer, it is possible you will inherit any problems you had on your old machine. For this reason, in your case, I would recommend the Dropbox solution. Personally, I use a combination of iCloud and Dropbox. And of course, if you need help, you can contact me, and I can help with the new set up. This article first appeared in the Post on March 31, 2021. articles.text: Phase 3 Communications is continuing construction work on Magnolia Avenue between Hillside and Highland Avenues, with an expected completion date by Friday, January 28. Utility work is being done in this section of Piedmont to expand better cell phone and internet access to residents. Crown Castle is the owner of the utility project and Phase 3 Communications is the general contractor installing the new system. Construction in this area began in July 2021, confirmed Phase 3 Communications Vice President Juan Carlos DeZubiria. Recent work on Magnolia Avenue began this week on Monday, January 17, and will continue through January 28. It is situated in the two blocks on Hillside and Magnolia Avenue from the Recreation Department to the Exedra. The company will bore in the street in front of the Recreation Dept. and Dress Best for Less carriage house on Bonita Avenue. The area will not be closed off to vehicular traffic, confirmed Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. Crews and flaggers will be on-site to direct traffic if needed, and work will be conducted from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays. Work will stop daily from 3 p.m. to 4 p.m. to accommodate school dismissals. A January 14 press release from the City of Piedmont noted the high volume of traffic in the area and urged motorists to avoid the area if possible. “The City realizes that this utility work in such a highly congested area adjacent to schools is not ideal,” said City Clerk John Tulloch. “Originally planned for late 2021, the work has been delayed to avoid conflicts in the area, including the School District’s ongoing construction, but unfortunately, it must be completed at this time.” “[Phase 3 Communications] did get approval to work later in the day, so we are hoping they will finish the work quickly,” Gonzales said. nationwide walkout that closed half of the primary schools in France.
